title: Two Wheels
subtitle: How the bicycle took almost a hundred years to reach its modern shape

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Today there are thought to be around a billion bicycles in the world, and for many people they are the cheapest and most practical way of getting around. Yet the bicycle took a surprisingly long time to develop. Many of the materials and techniques needed to build one existed by the eighteenth century, but it was not until the early 1800s that anyone produced a working two-wheeled machine, and almost another century passed before the bicycle took the form we recognise today. Its development also depended on a series of inventors, each building on the work of others, and on several false starts.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first step was taken in 1817 by Karl Drais, a forestry official in the German city of Mannheim. His 'running machine' had two wheels in a line, a wooden frame and a simple way of steering the front wheel, but no pedals: the rider sat astride it and pushed against the ground with his feet. Drais claimed that it allowed him to travel much faster than walking, and some historians have suggested that he was looking for an alternative to the horse after a series of poor harvests had made animal feed expensive. The machine enjoyed a brief period of popularity among wealthy young men in Europe, but it was banned from pavements in several cities, and interest soon faded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the 1860s, pedals were added directly to the front wheel, probably first in Paris, where the Michaux family began producing machines in large numbers. These 'velocipedes' were heavy, made of wood and iron, and their solid tyres gave such an uncomfortable ride on rough roads that in Britain they became known as “boneshakers”. Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, each turn of the pedals moved the machine only as far as the distance around that wheel. Riding one was hard work, and some towns even opened schools where people could learn to stay upright. To go faster, makers therefore began to build larger and larger front wheels.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The result, in the 1870s, was the high-wheeler, later nicknamed the penny-farthing because its huge front wheel and tiny rear one resembled a large and a small coin side by side. Some front wheels were up to one and a half metres across. Getting on and off required practice, and riders climbed up by stepping onto a small peg above the rear wheel. The machines were fast and, thanks to new wire-spoked wheels and solid rubber tyres, more comfortable than the boneshaker, but they were also dangerous. The rider sat high above the front wheel, and a sudden stop could throw him over the handlebars head first. Cycling became a sport for daring young men rather than a means of everyday transport.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The breakthrough came in 1885, when the English inventor John Kemp Starley produced the Rover. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that connected the pedals to the rear wheel, so that the rider sat much lower and could put their feet on the ground. Because the chain ran over gear wheels of different sizes, the rear wheel could turn faster than the pedals, removing the need for a giant front wheel. Three years later, in 1888, the Scottish vet John Boyd Dunlop developed an air-filled tyre, originally for his son's tricycle, which made riding far smoother. Together these inventions created what was called the 'safety bicycle', the basic design still used today.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The safety bicycle led to a cycling boom in the 1890s in Europe and North America. For the first time, large numbers of ordinary people could travel independently over long distances at little cost. The bicycle had a particular impact on women, who were able to travel without a companion, and it encouraged a move towards less restrictive clothing. Some critics at the time warned that cycling was unhealthy or improper for women, but campaigners for women's rights welcomed it as a symbol of independence. Historians still debate how great its social effects really were, but few doubt that it changed the lives of millions. Bicycle factories also developed techniques, such as ball bearings and light steel tubing, that were later used to build cars and aircraft; the Wright brothers, for example, ran a bicycle shop before they built their first aeroplane.
